instruments.evidence: Four files. The key state carries each member's public key instead of an id alone (GroupMember); rotation refuses with its own error while any member has published none; the handler maps that to 409; both test suites publish keys for their members, and a new test covers the keyless member.

37ee8ee76 (today's, the shared test router), af4bacefe (G1c), 800d8e003 (G1b), a848b585c (G1a). Also grepped every ledger for a member-public-key finding: the nearby ones (k4c1-public-key-session-only, k4b-partial-failure-orphans-keys) are about account keys, not group membership. This is new ground.

Printed the real key state for two materially different inputs. One member keyless: members:[{user_id:1,public_key:"public-key-for-1"},{user_id:2,public_key:""}]. Every member keyed: both carry their key. The state names who holds the group back; it does not merely omit them.

The real HTTP bodies, same two inputs: rotation with a keyless member answers 409 {"error":"A member has not set up encryption yet"}; once that member publishes a key the identical rotation answers 201 {"key_version":1}.

Read the SQL the state is built from: groupMembers LEFT JOINs users and COALESCEs the key to ''. Checked the schema rather than assuming: conversation_participants_user_id_fkey REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so a participant without a user row cannot exist and the LEFT JOIN guards a state the schema forbids today. It stays because an INNER JOIN would silently drop a member if that ever changed, and a dropped member is one nobody wraps a key for.
public_key carries the same value users.public_key holds, which is what the account-key path publishes and what importPublicKey reads on the client, so the two sides of the seam name the same bytes.
The shape change is caller-visible, so I looked for callers: no Go consumer outside the two test files, and the frontend has no group-key types yet (G2 is unwritten). Nothing receives the old []int.

instruments.why: No two implementations to run side by side.

instruments.evidence: The field is wired, not merely declared: the printed artifact carries real key values, and rotation changes its answer (409 against 201) on whether the field is empty.

The fixtures now match what a real producer emits. Every group-key test publishes keys for its members, through UserRepository.UpdatePublicKey in the integration suite. Before this the tests modelled a group whose members held no keys at all, which cannot occur in an encrypted group.
Real inputs that must pass: the all-keyed rotation answers 201, and the eight group-key unit tests pass.

Hostile inputs that must fail: a rotation naming a keyless member answers 409 and writes nothing, because the check runs before any INSERT; an outsider answers 403; copies that do not cover the members answer 400.
Boundaries: a group of one member; a member list where exactly one member of two lacks a key; a rotation for a version that is not the next one.

Compared the siblings that also wrap keys per recipient. modmail.go:385 tolerates a participant with no key and messages.go:712 does the same, both fail-closed: that participant cannot decrypt, nothing is exposed, and the frontend warns. A shared-key group cannot copy that: its copies must cover exactly the members, so skipping a keyless member would hand somebody a group they cannot read while the rest believe it is encrypted. Refusing is the consistent answer for a shared key, tolerating for a per-recipient one.

No branch became unreachable: containsInt is still used at line 283 for the history versions, and groupMembers and isGroupMember are both reached from groupKeyState. golangci-lint reports 0 issues, and it flags unused unexported functions.
Nothing is swallowed: the keyless case gets its own error rather than being folded into ErrGroupKeyCopies, which is the whole point of the change.

GetPublicKeysByIDs already exists, with one caller (handlers/auth.go:452). It is deliberately not reused here: the state needs the keys joined to the participants with COALESCE in a single query, through a querier that also runs inside the rotation transaction. A second round trip through the repository would read the members and their keys at two different moments.
Shape 'a member nobody wraps a key for': grepped every per-recipient key path in the backend (modmail, messages, search, message_recipient_keys). All of them fail closed, none exposes content.
Both packages under -race: 0 data races.
The keyless check runs inside the rotation transaction, before the first INSERT, and the deferred rollback leaves nothing behind. The existing test asserts that a refused rotation stores nothing.

instruments.evidence: Fed the guard the thing it exists to refuse, and then the thing it must accept: with one member keyless the rotation is refused with ErrGroupKeyNoPublicKey, and the identical rotation goes through once that member publishes a key. The new test asserts both halves, so a guard that always refused would fail it.
Measured rather than assumed, because a skipped package still prints ok: the eight group-key tests printed --- PASS under -v, and both packages reported 0 skipped.

The approved protocol says the server stores one copy per member, wrapped with that member's public key. Carrying those keys in the state is what lets a client do that at all, and refusing a keyless member keeps 'copies cover exactly the members' true instead of quietly weakening it.
State and Rotate read the members through one function, so the two entry points cannot disagree about who is in the group.
Every test that imports the changed code was run, not the tests beside it: the whole services package (ok 54.866s) and the whole integration package (ok 48.075s).
